notes.definition: The elements in Group 0 are the noble gases (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon). They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons, and their boiling points increase with increasing relative atomic mass.
explanation: Group 0 is the last column of the periodic table, on the far right. Its elements are called the noble gases: helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe) and radon (Rn). They are all colourless gases at room temperature and they are non-metals. Unlike the gases oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine, which exist as molecules of two atoms (O₂, N₂, Cl₂), the noble gases exist as single atoms. We say they are monatomic.

The noble gases are unreactive (inert) and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons. Neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon have eight electrons in their outer shell. Helium has only two electrons, but this still gives it a full outer shell because the first shell can hold only two electrons. Atoms of other elements react by losing, gaining or sharing electrons to obtain this kind of stable arrangement. A noble gas atom already has one, so it has no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.

Helium is placed in Group 0 even though it has only two outer electrons. This is because its properties match the rest of the group: it is an unreactive, monatomic gas with a full outer shell. Its position shows that the group is defined by stable, full outer shells rather than strictly by the number eight.

The boiling points of the noble gases increase going down the group, as the relative atomic mass increases. Helium boils at −269 °C, argon at −186 °C and radon at −62 °C. Going down the group the atoms become larger and heavier, so the forces of attraction between the atoms become stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point is higher. The density of the gases also increases down the group.

You can use these trends to predict properties. For example, if you know the boiling points of argon (−186 °C) and xenon (−108 °C), you can estimate that krypton, which lies between them, boils somewhere between these values (its actual boiling point is −153 °C). In exam questions you may be given a table of data with a missing value and asked to predict it from the pattern.

Because they are so unreactive, the noble gases are useful. Argon is used to fill filament lamps and to shield metals during welding, so that the hot metal does not react with oxygen. Helium is used in balloons and airships because it has a very low density and, unlike hydrogen, it does not burn. Neon is used in brightly coloured advertising signs.
keyFacts: Group 0 elements are called the noble gases.
They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules.
Their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons (full outer shells).
Noble gases have 8 electrons in the outer shell, except helium which has 2.
They exist as single atoms (monatomic), not molecules.
Boiling points increase going down the group as relative atomic mass increases.
Going down the group, atoms are larger so the forces between atoms are stronger.
All noble gases are colourless, non-metallic gases at room temperature.
Argon is used in lamps and welding; helium in balloons; neon in signs.

keyTerms.definition: The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon.
Not taking part in chemical reactions easily.
A full outer shell of electrons, which atoms have no tendency to change.
Existing as single, separate atoms rather than as molecules.
The highest occupied energy level in an atom; its electrons decide how the element reacts.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout the liquid.
The average mass of an element's atoms compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

workedExamples.title: Predicting a boiling point from a trend
workedExamples.question: The boiling point of argon is −186 °C and the boiling point of xenon is −108 °C. Krypton is between them in Group 0. Estimate the boiling point of krypton by assuming it is halfway between.
workedExamples.answer: About −147 °C (the actual value is −153 °C, so the estimate is reasonable).

workedExamples.title: Explaining unreactivity with electrons
workedExamples.question: Explain why argon (atomic number 18) is unreactive.
steps: Its outer shell contains 8 electrons, which is a full outer shell.
This is a stable arrangement, so argon atoms do not need to lose, gain or share electrons.
workedExamples.answer: Argon has a stable arrangement of electrons (8 in the outer shell), so it has no tendency to react.

workedExamples.title: Deciding the state of a noble gas
workedExamples.question: Radon has a boiling point of −62 °C. State whether radon is a solid, liquid or gas at 20 °C, and explain.
steps: 20 °C is above the boiling point of −62 °C.
Above its boiling point a substance is a gas.
workedExamples.answer: Radon is a gas at 20 °C because 20 °C is higher than its boiling point.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think helium is in Group 0 because it has 8 outer electrons.
misconceptions.right: In fact helium has only 2 electrons. Its outer (first) shell is full with 2, so it has a stable arrangement like the other noble gases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think noble gases exist as molecules such as He₂ or Ne₂.
misconceptions.right: In fact noble gases are monatomic: they exist as single atoms because they do not need to share electrons.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think boiling points go up down Group 0 because the covalent bonds get stronger.
misconceptions.right: In fact there are no covalent bonds. Boiling points increase because the forces of attraction between the atoms get stronger as the atoms get bigger.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think noble gases are unreactive because they are gases.
misconceptions.right: In fact many gases (oxygen, chlorine, hydrogen) are very reactive. Noble gases are unreactive because their atoms have full outer shells.

realWorld: Argon fills filament light bulbs so that the hot tungsten filament does not react with oxygen and burn away.
Argon is used as a shield gas in welding to stop the hot metal reacting with oxygen in the air.
Helium is used in party balloons and airships because it is less dense than air and, unlike hydrogen, it is not flammable.
Neon gives the red glow in advertising signs when electricity is passed through it.
examTips: Say 'stable arrangement of electrons' or 'full outer shell'. Do not say noble gases have 'full shells' without saying 'outer'.
Remember the exception: helium has 2 outer electrons, not 8.
When explaining the boiling point trend, refer to forces between atoms getting stronger as atoms get larger, never to bonds breaking.
For prediction questions, show your working (for example taking the mean of the values either side) and give units.
summary: Group 0 elements are the noble gases.
They are unreactive because their atoms have full outer shells (stable arrangements of electrons).
They have 8 outer electrons, except helium, which has 2.
Boiling points increase down the group as relative atomic mass increases.

questions.question: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
options: They are gases at room temperature
Their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: stable arrangement of electrons / full outer shell
questions.explanation: A full outer shell means there is no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons. Being a gas does not make a substance unreactive; chlorine is a reactive gas.

questions.question: How many electrons does a helium atom have in its outer shell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2
questions.explanation: Helium has only 2 electrons, which fill its first and only shell. All the other noble gases have 8.

questions.question: What happens to the boiling points of the noble gases going down Group 0?
markScheme: 1 mark: they increase
questions.explanation: Boiling points rise from helium (−269 °C) to radon (−62 °C) as relative atomic mass increases.

questions.question: How do noble gases exist?
markScheme: 1 mark: as single atoms
questions.explanation: Noble gases are monatomic because their atoms are already stable and do not bond to each other.

questions.question: Which is the electronic structure of argon (atomic number 18)?
questions.explanation: 18 electrons fill shells as 2, 8, 8. 2,8,7 is chlorine (17) and 2,8,8,1 is potassium (19).

questions.question: Which noble gas has the highest boiling point?
markScheme: 1 mark: radon
questions.explanation: Radon is at the bottom of the group with the largest relative atomic mass, so it has the highest boiling point.

questions.question: Why is helium, rather than hydrogen, used to fill party balloons?
options: Helium is unreactive so it does not burn
Helium forms He₂ molecules that are very light
Helium is a liquid at room temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: unreactive / does not burn
questions.explanation: Both gases are less dense than air, but hydrogen is flammable. Helium is unreactive and monatomic.

questions.question: Argon is used inside filament lamps. What is the reason?
options: It is unreactive, so the hot filament does not react with it
It reacts with the filament to protect it
markScheme: 1 mark: unreactive
questions.explanation: The very hot tungsten filament would react with oxygen and burn away. Argon is unreactive so it protects the filament.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why the boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group?
options: The covalent bonds between atoms get stronger
The atoms gain more outer electrons
The forces of attraction between atoms get stronger as the atoms get larger
markScheme: 1 mark: stronger forces between atoms as atoms get larger
questions.explanation: There are no covalent bonds in noble gases. All have full outer shells. Larger atoms attract each other more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.question: Krypton and chlorine are both gases. Chlorine is very reactive but krypton is not. Which statement explains this difference?
options: Chlorine atoms need one more electron to fill the outer shell, but krypton atoms have a full outer shell
Krypton atoms are smaller than chlorine atoms
Chlorine has a higher boiling point than krypton
Krypton atoms have more protons, which stops them reacting
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine needs 1 electron, krypton outer shell full
questions.explanation: Chlorine (2,8,7) readily gains an electron. Krypton has 8 outer electrons, a stable arrangement. Krypton atoms are larger, not smaller.

questions.question: Give the number of electrons in the outer shell of a neon atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: 8
questions.explanation: Neon is 2,8. Its outer shell holds 8 electrons.

questions.question:
Xenon has atomic number 54.
Give the number of electrons in a xenon atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: 54
questions.explanation: In an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, which is the atomic number.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the boiling points of helium and radon.
Calculate the difference between the two boiling points.
markScheme: 1 mark: 207 °C
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative number adds: −62 + 269 = 207 °C. Check: 269 − 62 = 207.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the boiling points of three noble gases. Krypton is between argon and xenon in Group 0.
Estimate the boiling point of krypton.
Assume it is halfway between the boiling points of argon and xenon.
markScheme: 1 mark: −147 °C (accept −144 to −150)
questions.explanation: The mean of −186 and −108 is −294 ÷ 2 = −147 °C. The real value is −153 °C, so the trend is not exactly linear.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes in a sample of neon.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of neon in this sample.
markScheme: 1 mark: 20.2
questions.explanation: (1800 + 220) ÷ 100 = 2020 ÷ 100 = 20.2. The answer is closer to 20 because most atoms are neon-20.

questions.question: State why the noble gases are unreactive.
markScheme: 1 mark: they have a stable arrangement of electrons / full outer shell
questions.explanation: Their atoms do not need to lose, gain or share electrons.

questions.question: Name the noble gas with the lowest boiling point.
markScheme: 1 mark: helium
questions.explanation: Helium is at the top of the group with the smallest relative atomic mass, so it has the lowest boiling point (−269 °C).

questions.question: Explain why the noble gases exist as single atoms instead of molecules.
markScheme: 1 mark: their atoms already have a full outer shell / stable arrangement of electrons
1 mark: so they do not need to share electrons / form covalent bonds with each other
questions.explanation: Molecules form when atoms share electrons to fill their outer shells. Noble gas atoms are already full.

questions.question:

Helium has only two electrons in its outer shell.

questions.question: Explain why xenon has a higher boiling point than neon.
markScheme: 1 mark: xenon atoms are larger / have a greater relative atomic mass
1 mark: so the forces of attraction between xenon atoms are stronger
1 mark: so more energy is needed to overcome these forces
questions.explanation: The explanation must refer to forces between atoms, not bonds within atoms.

questions.question: Suggest why the noble gases were discovered much later than most other elements.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are unreactive so do not form compounds that can be detected
1 mark: they are colourless, odourless gases present in only small amounts in air
questions.explanation: Most elements were found from their compounds. Noble gases form almost none and are hard to notice.

questions.question: Give one use of argon.
markScheme: 1 mark: filling filament lamps / shield gas in welding
questions.explanation: Both uses rely on argon being unreactive.

questions.question: Describe and explain the properties of the noble gases. Use ideas about electronic structure in your answer and include the trend in boiling points.
markScheme: Indicative content: noble gases are in Group 0; colourless gases at room temperature; non-metals; unreactive (inert); do not easily form molecules (monatomic); atoms have a stable arrangement of electrons / full outer shell; 8 outer electrons, helium has 2 (first shell full); no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons; boiling points low; boiling points increase down the group as relative atomic mass increases; atoms larger so forces between atoms stronger, more energy needed; uses linked to unreactivity, such as argon in lamps and helium in balloons.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed description of properties with clear explanations linked to electronic structure, and a correct explanation of the boiling point trend.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes several properties with some explanation in terms of electrons or the trend.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'unreactive' or 'gases' with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Link each property to its cause: full outer shell explains unreactivity and monatomic nature; atom size explains the boiling point trend.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows data for some noble gases.
Describe the trends shown in Table 1.
Predict the boiling point of xenon and explain the trend in boiling point.
markScheme: Indicative content: boiling point increases as relative atomic mass increases; density increases down the group; predicted boiling point of xenon between about −130 °C and −90 °C (actual −108 °C), justified from the pattern (rises of 60 °C and 33 °C); explanation: atoms get larger down the group, so forces of attraction between atoms get stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both trends described, a sensible prediction with justification, and a correct explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one trend described or a prediction with little justification.
questions.explanation: A sensible prediction is higher than krypton's −153 °C. The explanation needs forces between atoms.

questions.question:
Argon is in Group 0 and potassium is in Group 1. They are next to each other in the periodic table.
Figure 1 shows the electronic structures of an argon atom and a potassium atom.
Compare the reactivity of argon and potassium.
In your answer you should:
• explain why one element is very reactive and the other is not
• explain why argon is used to protect hot metals during welding.

markScheme: Indicative content: argon 2,8,8, potassium 2,8,8,1; argon has a full outer shell, a stable arrangement, so it does not lose, gain or share electrons and is unreactive; potassium has one outer electron, which is far from the nucleus and easily lost; potassium forms K⁺ (2,8,8), the same arrangement as argon; so potassium is very reactive (reacts vigorously with water and oxygen); argon is monatomic and inert; in welding, hot metal would react with oxygen in air; argon surrounds the metal, keeping oxygen away, and does not react with the hot metal itself.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): accurate electronic structures, clear comparison explaining reactivity of both, and a well-reasoned explanation of the welding use.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct structures with some explanation of the difference in reactivity, or of the welding use.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'argon is unreactive' or 'potassium is reactive', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The key insight is that K⁺ ends up with argon's stable arrangement, which is why potassium reacts and argon does not.
